one_liner: Header-only C++20 single-source kernel layer (CUDA, HIP, SYCL, OpenMP, TBB) matching native BabelStream bandwidth on GH200 and Grace.
what_it_does: alpaka is a performance-portability layer: you write one kernel as a function object, enqueue it on a queue for a device, and pick a backend (CUDA, HIP, SYCL/oneAPI, OpenMP blocks, TBB blocks or serial) at configure time. alpaka3, on the default dev_v3.x branch, is a redesign with a new API (onHost::/onAcc:: namespaces, frame specs, SIMD packs, primitives such as iota, fill, transform, reduce and transformReduce) and is not source-compatible with the 1.x/2.x releases. It is not a BLAS: it replaces hand-written CUDA/HIP/OpenMP code, not OpenBLAS or cuBLAS calls.
how_it_is_fast: Kernels are compiled straight to the native model of each backend, so there is no runtime dispatch layer in the hot loop. alpaka3's index domain is split into equally sized frames, and onAcc::SimdAlgo::concurrent walks each frame with explicit SIMD packs (load, fill, vector arithmetic) per worker thread, which lets compilers emit wide loads and stores on CPUs where mainline alpaka's one-element-per-thread mapping did not. The BabelStream port uses 512 threads per block and a per-device elements-per-thread factor; reductions go through the library's transformReduce.
when_to_use: You maintain a C++ code that must run on NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs plus multi-core CPUs and want one kernel source instead of CUDA, HIP, SYCL and OpenMP variants.

Memory-bound streaming kernels (copy, scale, add, triad, dot style) where the target is native-code bandwidth: the project shows 99% of the NVIDIA reference on a GH200 GPU and 107% on a Grace CPU with 72 OpenMP threads.

HPC codes already built around alpaka (the group's particle-in-cell work is cited in CITATION.cff) that want the alpaka3 SIMD/frame API and its CPU dot-product fix (447 GB/s vs 40 GB/s for mainline alpaka on Grace).
Teams that want to unit-test GPU kernels on a CPU-only CI machine with the serial or OpenMP backend.
when_not_to_use: You need dense linear algebra (GEMM, LU, QR): alpaka provides no BLAS routines; use a vendor BLAS, OpenBLAS, BLIS or CLBlast.

You need a stable, released API today: alpaka3 has no release tag (CITATION.cff says 3.0.0, the latest tag is mainline 2.2.0 from 2026-10-08), and its install docs still point to alpaka-group/alpaka3 branch dev.

Compute-bound kernels that depend on vendor-specific features (tensor cores, warp intrinsics, cooperative groups): BabelStream only shows bandwidth parity, and explicit shared-memory caching is left to the kernel author.
Windows or macOS builds: the README badge lists Linux only.

Codes that need bitwise-reproducible reductions: the docs say thread reordering makes deterministic results impossible to guarantee, and issue #2434 (open) notes dot-product verification drift on single-threaded backends.

integration.dependencies: none for the core; CMake 3.25+ (alpaka_finalize target helper); the CUDA Toolkit, ROCm/HIP, oneAPI, OpenMP or TBB for the chosen backend; Catch2 for tests and benchmarks
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (g++, clang++, nvcc or icpx); CMake 3.25; the GPU chart used CUDA 13.3 and the CPU chart GNU 14.3
integration.platforms: Linux; x86, ARM, RISC-V and Power8+ CPUs; NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs
integration.thread_safety: not documented beyond the queue/event model (work is ordered within a queue; separate queues may run concurrently); recent commits fix deadlocks in blocking host queues

gotchas: Harness asymmetry: the alpaka3 BabelStream port (benchmark/babelstream/src/babelStreamCommon.hpp) computes bandwidth from the minimum time over runs 2..N, while the GPU chart says the NVIDIA reference values are 'the mean of supplied runs'; neither chart names the reference code, its flags or its run count, so the 107%/99% ratios compare best-of-N against figures of unknown aggregation that the project did not re-run.

The Grace CPU reference bars (about 408 GB/s for Add and Triad) sit at or below the low end of NVIDIA's own expected STREAM Triad range for a GH200 Grace with 72 threads (410 to 486 GB/s, from a search snippet of NVIDIA's Grace tuning guide; the page itself was unreachable), while alpaka3's 456 GB/s sits inside it, so the 7% CPU win may reflect a weak reference run rather than a better kernel.

In the same harness the NStream kernel (a += b + scalar*c touches four arrays) is credited with only two arrays of traffic, so its reported bandwidth is half the true figure; the README charts do not use NStream.

The benchmark sources carry BabelStream's licence, whose clause 3b requires results from modified code to be labelled as a BabelStream variant; the README charts are titled 'BabelStream performance' without that label.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the blas-lapack siblings is a kernel-portability layer: pick alpaka when you write your own kernels and need one source for CUDA, HIP, SYCL and OpenMP; pick CLBlast or a vendor BLAS (OpenBLAS, MKL, cuBLAS) when what you need is GEMM-class routines.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README charts from JUPITER (Juelich): on a Grace CPU (OpenMP, 72 threads, GNU 14.3, -ftree-vectorize -mcpu=neoverse-v2) alpaka3's BabelStream port reaches 469/469/453/456 GB/s on Copy/Mult/Add/Triad, 107% of an unnamed NVIDIA reference on average (reference bars about 455/458/408/408 GB/s, derived from page data); on a GH200 GPU (CUDA 13.3, flags not stated) it reaches 3,636 to 3,667 GB/s, 99% of the reference, i.e. parity. Dot has no reference; versus mainline alpaka it is 447 vs 40 GB/s on the CPU and 3,731 vs 3,678 GB/s on the GPU, all double precision at 2^30 elements.
status_note: Actively developed (dev_v3.x commits on 2026-10-01, 214 open issues, 428 stars) and MPL-2.0, but alpaka3 is unreleased and its API differs from the released 2.x line, so pin a commit if you adopt it now.
sources_read: WebSearch: NVIDIA Grace CPU BabelStream OpenMP results (snippets of docs.nvidia.com/grace-perf-tuning-guide/health-checks.html; the page itself returned ENOTFOUND)
